newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia plans no new military bloc-defence minister.
newsitem.headline: Russia plans no new military bloc-defence minister.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said on Thursday that Russia, keen to avoid new global confrontation, was not planning to respond to NATO's eastward expansion by creating its own new military bloc.

Just days before NATO Secretary General Javier Solana visits Moscow, Rodionov told a news conference that Russia strongly opposed the Western alliance's plans to enlarge but did not regard it as an immediate foe.
"If NATO wants to expand let it expand, but we are against this," he said. "For our part we are not going to expand and it does not seem we are going to set up any new military bloc."
In a reference to the Cold War years, he said: "This could only lead to a revival of the situation which kept the world in fear for decades."

During a visit to Vienna on Thursday, Solana told reporters he wanted to have negotiations on bilateral relations with Russia "on target" by the time of the Atlantic alliance's next summit in Madrid in July.
"We don't know when we will be able to finish this exercise but we are going to start soon. We hope to have it on target by the time of the summit," Solana said.

Last week, Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who is in hospital recovering from pneumonia, reiterated Moscow's tough opposition to NATO's planned expansion and told his government to work out its response if and when enlargement occurred.
Rodionov, 60, a career officer who became Russia's first civilian defence minister after leaving active military service last year, did not say what counter-measures might be taken.
"We are doing nothing," he said. "The defence ministry is monitoring the situation and preparing its proposals."

Asked whether he saw the possibility of forming a military alliance with Belarus, the former Soviet republic whose leaders and population have expressed interest in stronger ties with Russia, Rodionov replied: "For the time being I am against any defence alliance."
"But this is for the supreme political leadership to decide," he added.

Rodionov said his ministry was monitoring potential military threats to Russia's security from various directions, including the West. But he said this was normal for any defence ministry and did not mean he viewed any specific country as an immediate foe.
"Russia faces potential threats from the west, south and east," he said replying to the question whether he saw NATO's expansion as a threat to Russia. "But these are potential threats, not enemies."

NATO, which is expected to make a final decision later this year on admitting some of Moscow's Cold War allies as members, is trying to ease Russia's fears that such moves would threaten its security.
Solana is due to to hold talks in Moscow on Monday with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, who has demanded a say for Russia in decisions which it believes affect its national interests.
Independent analysts say Moscow is keen to win as many concessions as possible before NATO enlargement goes ahead.

A U.S. newspaper on Thursday quoted NATO diplomats as saying the alliance had prepared a package of offers for Moscow which would include new flexibility on arms control problems, greater economic assistance and a special consultative status.

The Washington Post said the consulting role would give Russia a seat at NATO's table in mulling policy on common problems such as nuclear proliferation, regional defence, terrorism, international crime and peacekeeping.
